title: Land that could not support both herds
summary: Genesis links the size of Abram and Lot’s holdings with land unable to support them together. Grazing science likewise relates the number of animals an area can sustain to its available resources.
text: KJV Genesis 13:5: “had flocks, and herds, and tents”. KJV Genesis 13:6: “And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.” KJV Genesis 13:7: “a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle”. KJV Genesis 13:9: “separate thyself, I pray thee, from me”. NDSU Extension’s carrying-capacity guide, hosted by USDA NRCS, relates the livestock an area can sustain to forage supply and animal demand, with water and other site conditions also affecting stocking rates.
reasoning: The passage identifies flocks and herds before attributing the difficulty of remaining together to the size of their holdings. That limited resource constraint agrees with the documented need to balance livestock demand with available grazing resources. The science source does not independently establish the reported dispute or prove that grazing shortage was its only cause.
scope: Agreement concerns the general resource constraint, not a measured carrying capacity for this location. A broader reading may include space, access rights and social conflict as well as pasture; the passage gives no herd counts, acreage, forage measurements or water budget. The guide concerns modern North Dakota management, so its local stocking figures are not transferred to Genesis. No event, date or sole cause is reconstructed, and the wider passage receives no scientific verdict.

sources.label: NDSU Extension / USDA NRCS · Carrying capacity and stocking rates, pp. 1–2

fields.text: The guide distinguishes livestock forage demand from the forage a piece of land can provide. Supporting more animals requires sufficient resources; capacity varies with conditions. Only that general relation is compared here, without calculating an ancient stocking rate.

title: Sarah’s late pregnancy and reproductive aging
summary: Sarah is described as old, with the usual female cycle ceased, before her later conception. The narrative attributes the birth to God’s promise and gives no physiological mechanism.
text: KJV Genesis 17:17: “and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?” KJV Genesis 18:11: “it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women”. KJV Genesis 18:14: “Is any thing too hard for the Lord?” KJV Genesis 21:1: “And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said”. KJV Genesis 21:2: “For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age”. MedlinePlus describes menopause as the end of menstrual periods and natural fertility, recognized after twelve months without a period. The narrative supplies no menstrual timeline sufficient for that clinical comparison or an ordinary explanation of the subsequent conception.
reasoning: If the description in Genesis 18:11 refers to the end of menstruation, it supplies reproductive-aging context for why the promised birth is presented as exceptional. Modern information about menopause does not by itself diagnose Sarah, establish a natural conception mechanism in this account or test the divine action it attributes. Context preserves that distinction rather than treating an unspecified miracle as a scientifically disproved event.
scope: The comparison depends on reading the KJV’s manner-of-women wording as menstruation; no original-language lexical finding is claimed. A literary or theological account and miraculous intervention remain possible readings, not scientifically established explanations. The passage is not a clinical case history, and age alone is not used here to diagnose menopause or calculate fertility. No historical event or treatment is reconstructed, and the record gives no verdict on the whole passage.

sources.label: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine · Menopause

fields.text: MedlinePlus distinguishes the transition toward menopause from menopause itself. A statement that periods have ceased lacks the duration needed for the clinical definition; the biblical account also attributes the later conception to divine action rather than describing an ordinary reproductive process.
